analysis.title: US Economics Analyst: The Causes and Consequences of a Low-Hire, Low-Fire Labor Market
key_insights: The US labor market has settled into a low-hire, low-fire form of full employment, with hiring, quits and layoff rates all below pre-pandemic levels.
Low turnover is the main reason GS's slack tracker, a composite of ten measures, signals a labor market somewhat softer than the unemployment rate alone suggests.
Job reallocation has declined since the late 1990s but the decline has slowed. It sits just 0.2pp below its 2015-2019 average, so it explains little of the recent turnover slowdown.
Churn, worker flows between existing jobs, explains most of the recent turnover decline. It is almost 1pp below its 2015-2019 average and has run unusually low since last year.
Structural drivers of lower churn are an aging workforce and better worker-firm matches. Temporary drivers are post-pandemic settling down of job-switching and an emerging AI effect.

Churn has fallen further below pre-pandemic levels in industries with greater AI adoption and automation potential. The labor market perception indicator has deteriorated sharply since last year despite a stable unemployment rate, with a sharper drop among young workers.

Reduced turnover is modestly hurting job finding. Job-finding rates have fallen more in low-churn industries and states, and unemployment spells have lengthened roughly twice as much there. Little evidence that early-career workers are faring disproportionately worse.
GS estimates depressed churn is weighing on year-over-year wage growth by about 0.3pp, with the GS wage tracker slightly below 3.5%.
GS expects turnover to pick up somewhat as post-pandemic normalization and AI uncertainty fade. If low turnover persists, productivity growth could be dampened by fewer better worker-firm matches.
GS forecast table shows unemployment at 4.2% through 2027, core PCE 2.4% by Q4 2027, and an FF target range of 4-4.25% by Q4 2027.

macro_indicators.indicator: Wage growth drag from low churn
macro_indicators.interpretation: GS model estimate that subdued turnover holds wage growth down even given the unemployment rate, which is mildly disinflationary for services.
Nominal wage growth is subdued, consistent with softer labor market dynamics.
Reallocation explains little of the recent turnover decline.
Churn is the main source of the turnover decline.
GS forecasts a stable unemployment rate while turnover stays low.
GS table path for policy rate.

risk_factors: Persistently low turnover could lock out the unemployed and lengthen unemployment spells.
Low dynamism could dampen productivity growth by hindering better worker-firm matches.
AI-related job insecurity could keep churn and wage growth depressed longer than expected.
Perceived labor market weakness may be understated by the unemployment rate.

theme_stances.key_argument: Depressed churn, partly from AI job insecurity, is modestly weighing on job finding and wage growth, though GS expects turnover to recover somewhat.

theme_stances.key_argument: Churn has fallen further in industries with greater AI adoption and automation potential as workers stay put amid rising job insecurity.
